transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Carlos (EmberTech Head ML), Priya (Platform Eng), Sam (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Walked EmberTech through Redwood model catalog and how to select open models for a low-latency customer-facing assistant.
- Demoed console model filters, compatibility matrix, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization.
- Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) tradeoffs, security/KMS and audit log needs.
- Agreed next steps: share benchmark template, schedule pilot baseline week, provide SOC2/security pack.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, I'm on the AE side, joining with Maya who's our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:04] Carlos: Good, hey thanks, Carlos here. Excited, we want to get into model selection and benching today, so good timing.
[00:09] Priya: Hi, Priya. We'll be focused on platform constraints — open to hearing about the console filters too.
[00:13] Sam: Sam here, I'll be listening for security stuff, KMS, audit logs, data residency.
[00:16] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda: Maya will demo the model catalog — filters, bench results, compat matrix — then we'll show Optimize suggestions, and end with deployment options and Q&A. Sound good?
[00:25] Carlos: Yep, go for it.

[02:10] Maya: Alright starting the demo. So here is the catalog view in the console — you can filter by architecture (decoder/encoder), tokenizer type, quantization level, and hardware compatibility. The table shows latency bench results from our internal runs and community-contributed benches.
[02:35] Maya: For EmberTech's use case you said low-latency chat with about 1–2k token context and lots of short completions, so we recommend models that have strong per-token latency and good KV cache behavior.
[02:50] Carlos: Right, our assistant is customer-facing so P95 latency matters more than raw throughput. Cost is a concern but SLA comes first.
[02:58] Maya: Understood. If I toggle the 'compatibility matrix' view here, you can see per-model which kernels are available on which GPUs, whether continuous-batching is supported, and quantized variants.
[03:15] Jordan: Quick note — the compat matrix also shows fallback compatibility. So if a preferred model or GPU isn't available the router can fall back to a compatible variant automatically.
[03:27] Priya: That fallback bit is important. If we schedule dedicated capacity in us-east-1, can requests fail over to hosted? We need cross-region fallback.
[03:36] Maya: Yes, we can route by policy: latency SLO first, then cost. You can pin a policy that prefers dedicated but allows hosted fallback to keep the SLA. Cross-region fallbacks are supported, though you'd pay for egress if crossing regions.
[03:52] Sam: Do fallbacks leak any customer data into the hosted environment? From a compliance pov we need clarity.
[03:58] Jordan: Good point — we have routing policies that preserve data handling constraints. For EmberTech you could set policy 'no hosted fallback' for sensitive routes. We'll document the exact headers and egress paths in the security pack.

[05:10] Maya: Back to the catalog: I'm going to apply a filter for 8-bit quantized variants and show bench rows. Notice these two models — 'open-7b-v3-q8' and 'atlas-chat-8b-q4' — show P95 token latency ~120ms vs ~80ms on the same GPU family. The 'atlas' variant has optimized kernels on Ampere+ and a smaller KV overhead.
[05:37] Carlos: Interesting. The names sometimes are off in the transcript like 'atlas' here sounds like what we saw in your research notes, but can you annotate where the bench came from?
[05:45] Maya: Yep each bench row links back to the run artifacts — there's a link to the bench spreadsheet and the kernel mapping. Example link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/EMB-4821/run-20270110
[05:58] Priya: Are those bench numbers from your hosted fleet or from dedicated hardware? We care about variance across instances.
[06:04] Maya: The catalog shows combined artifacts but you can filter to only dedicated runs. For the 'atlas-chat' numbers I'm showing those are from our dedicated testing on NVIDIA A10s; hosted numbers are slightly higher in P95 due to multi-tenant noise.
[06:17] Jordan: Also Optimize will suggest quant levels and batching config based on your prompt distribution; it's not one-size-fits-all.

[07:30] Carlos: Walk me through a typical bench plan. We want repeatable results and to avoid the common traps.
[07:36] Maya: Good question. We have a benchmark template that expects three prompt buckets: short queries (<50 tokens), medium (50–300), and long (300–2k). You provide token distribution and expected concurrency. We run baseline on hosted and dedicated, then we run with prefix caching enabled and with recommended quantization. The output CSV includes P50/P95 latency, tokens/sec, and per-token cost estimate.
[07:59] Carlos: Can we run it on-prem? We might do private deployment in a data center.
[08:05] Maya: We support private deployments. For on-prem you'll run a local collector bench runner that mimics the exact requests; we'll provide a Dockerized harness. The console accepts uploaded bench artifacts so we can interpret the results centrally.

[09:20] Priya: Regarding Optimize suggestions — does it just recommend batching sizes or does it also recommend kernel/quant combos?
[09:27] Maya: Both. Optimize ingests your workload and suggests a profile: target batch window, max tokens per batch, cache TTL for prefixes, and a recommended quantization profile per model family. It will also flag models where kernel mapping is suboptimal and recommend an alternative variant.
[09:42] Jordan: For example, it might say 'use atlas-chat-8b-q4 for PTX kernel family X on A10; fallback to open-7b-v3-q8 for CPU fallback', stuff like that.

[11:00] Sam: Security — how are keys managed for Private deployment? We need KMS/HSM integration, and audit logs for inference requests.
[11:09] Maya: For private we support customer-managed keys via KMS, and we can integrate with on-prem HSMs. Audit logs include request metadata (route, model, timestamp) and optionally redacted tokens. Full transcripts are not stored by default unless you enable retention.
[11:27] Sam: Good. Also need RBAC for model access and ability to lock down fallback routes.
[11:32] Jordan: Yep RBAC is in the Console — you can grant route-level perms and separate billing from access. We'll include screenshots in the security pack.

[13:45] Carlos: Quick question on cost modeling. Your per-token cost estimate — is that only the compute token cost or does it include infra overheads like orchestration and egress?
[13:54] Maya: The initial estimate includes raw per-token compute and amortized infra per-request overhead. There's a detailed breakdown in the bench CSV: compute, network, storage, and a line item for orchestration overhead depending on config (e.g., whether caching is enabled).
[14:10] Priya: If we enable KV prefix caching how does that affect accuracy? We can't allow stale contexts.
[14:18] Maya: Prefix caching is exact for repeated prefixes and you control TTL. For chat scenarios we do token-range invalidation; usually TTL is short for user conversation features. Optimize will simulate the hit rate and show expected cost savings vs increased staleness risk.

[16:05] Jordan: I want to demo a short bench run in the console — I'll switch to the run viewer. You'll see the run timeline, kernel selection per step, and the mapping table where it picked alternate kernels for long sequences.
[16:24] Maya: Notice here the compat matrix flagged that atlas-chat-8b-q4 doesn't have a fused attention kernel on older Ampere variants; that's why its P95 jumps at 1.5k tokens. The matrix suggests open-7b-v3-q8 for older hardware.
[16:44] Carlos: Hmm that makes sense. We have a mixed fleet in us-east and us-west; some nodes are older. Can the router do per-model device selection?
[16:52] Maya: Yes — you can set device affinity rules. E.g., prefer 'atlas' on 'A100/A10s' and for older devices route to 'open-7b-v3' variants. That's in the routing policy UI.

[18:30] Carlos: For the pilot, we want a canary rollout: 10% of traffic on dedicated, then 50%. Can you support staged traffic with automatic rollback?
[18:37] Jordan: Yes rollouts are supported — you can define canary steps and auto-fallback thresholds based on latency or error rates. We'll also instrument traces back to your app.

[20:00] Priya: Any caveats around quantization impacting hallucination rates? We need to maintain answer quality for compliance checks.
[20:08] Maya: Quant can change some model behavior. In our bench artifacts we include quality checks against your eval prompt set — BLEU-ish metrics and some classifier-based checks. We recommend running your eval set across quant variants during the bench.
[20:25] Carlos: We'll definitely upload our evals.

[22:10] Sam: A couple security SOP items: we need proof of SOC2 Type II and the retention policy for request payloads, plus an ATO template.
[22:19] Jordan: We'll send the SOC2 report and an architecture note. For retention we default to 30 days for logs and 90 days for metrics, but you can change that in Private. We'll include the ATO checklist.

[25:00] Maya: Jumping back to the catalog, one zinger we added recently is a 'compatibility delta' column — it surfaces how much latency changes between hosted/dedicated/quant variants for the same token length. It's a quick way to shortlist models.
[25:20] Carlos: Nice. That would speed our pruning.

[27:10] Jordan: Let's talk timeline: you said Q1 pilot — what's your target go-live and internal signoffs?
[27:17] Carlos: We want a production pilot by end of Q1, with security signoff before then. Timeline is tight but doable if benching goes well.
[27:27] Priya: We also need a cost projection for 100k monthly active users, with expected token mix — we'll share a spreadsheet with estimated usage.
[27:35] Jordan: Perfect — include that in the bench input and we'll return a cost-modeled projection.

[30:00] Maya: I'm going to demo Optimize's suggestion card for a sample workload. It suggests batch window 20ms, max batch size 8 for short queries, and a quant profile of q4 for atlas-chat for best latency/cost. It also shows the expected P95 improvements and cost delta.
[30:22] Carlos: That card — can we export it as a JSON config to feed into our infra?
[30:28] Maya: Yes, every Optimize profile can be exported as a JSON policy that configures batch settings, quant preference, and routing rules.

[32:40] Priya: About observability — how granular are traces? We want token-level timing edges for performance debugging.
[32:48] Maya: We provide per-request spans: request enter, kernel selection, token-gen windows and KV cache hits. Token-level is available but is redacted by default unless you enable debug retention.

[35:10] Carlos: On the catalog UI, can we pin models to a route so product teams don't accidentally swap experiments?
[35:18] Jordan: Yes route binding and model pinning are features — you can make a model immutable for a route and only allow SE to change it. RBAC applies.

[38:00] Sam: One more on compliance: If we use hosted fallbacks are logs retained in Redwood cloud? We might require logs to be forwarded to our SIEM only.
[38:08] Maya: Hosted fallbacks will have logs in Redwood's control plane unless you enable log forwarding. We support forwarding to Splunk/Datadog or an S3 bucket in your account. For private you can keep everything in your VPC.

[40:15] Carlos: Ok, assuming we do benching next week, what's the minimum data you need from us?
[40:21] Maya: Three sample prompt sets, token distribution CSV, concurrency profile (typical and peak), and any eval prompts for quality checks. Also tell us which regions and hardware targets you prefer.

[42:00] Jordan: I'll recap and propose dates. We will: share the bench template and a runbook today, propose pilot baseline week Jan 25–29, and Maya will provision a short-lived Dedicated endpoint for your tests.
[42:20] Priya: Works for me.
[42:23] Carlos: Yep.
[42:25] Sam: Please add the SOC2 and KMS integration docs to the share.
[42:28] Jordan: Will do.

[45:10] Maya: Quick demo note — when you upload bench artifacts the console will auto-tag kernel mismatches and produce a 'compatibility risk' score. That score factors into Optimize recommendations.
[45:28] Carlos: Good. We'll look at that risk score when reviewing the run.

[48:00] Jordan: Any more questions?
[48:05] Priya: One small thing — do you support cloud provider affinity so we can keep workloads in the same cloud as our services?
[48:13] Maya: Yes you can prefer provider affinity in routing rules and even pin to a dedicated capacity in a specific region and cloud.

[50:00] Carlos: Thanks everyone — this was very practical.
[50:05] Sam: Thanks.
[50:07] Jordan: Great. Quick recap of actions: Jordan shares bench template and security pack by Jan 18; Maya provisions endpoint and runs initial perf sweep by Jan 22; Carlos uploads prompt sets by Jan 17. We'll aim for pilot Jan 25–29.
[50:25] Jordan: I'm going to drop links in the calendar invite and the shared Drive. Links: bench template: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/EMB-4821/template.csv ; security pack: https://redwood.ai/security/EMB-4821/pack.pdf
[50:42] Carlos: Received.
[50:45] Priya: Thanks, we'll review.
[50:47] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email and put the next call on the calendar.
[50:52] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard model names (e.g., "atlas" transcribed as "Atlus" in raw audio), proper nouns sometimes off, timestamps are approximate.
